clue.text: Park sown from this?

parts.note: surface reading: a park grown from seed scattered over it
setter's reading: take the little word AND out of the racecourse's name and SOWN is left behind

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a park was grown from a particular patch of seed.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: S-AND-OWN minus AND leaves SOWN, so the answer is the word from which 'sown' comes. Sandown Park is a racecourse in Surrey, like the other courses in this grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandown Park is the full name of the Surrey racecourse, so the single word Park points to its first half.

clue.text: Puzzle over, is working overtime entertaining?

indicators.note: a host entertaining guests has them inside the house, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: read as 'over time': an age is a long stretch of time
a machine that is working is on
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person putting in extra hours is fun to watch while they wrestle with a problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overtime' looks like extra hours at work, but it has to be read loosely as a long span of time, which then holds the working words.
explanation.definitionFit: To agonise over something is to worry and deliberate about it at length, much as one puzzles over a problem.

clue.text: Ones that block terminal keyboard shift keys

indicators.note: a terminal is an end point, so only the final letter is wanted

parts.note: the final letter of this word

indicators.note: to shift things is to move them about, so the letters change places

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint about the shift keys on a computer keyboard jamming up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terminal keyboard shift keys' reads like computer jargon, but it splits into the last letter of keyboard plus a rearrangement of KEYS.
explanation.definitionFit: Dykes are embankments built to hold back the sea or a river, so they are things that block water.

clue.text: Scrubbers' rings

definitions.meaning: first meaning: people or machines that clean things

definitions.note: plural noun; the clue's first meaning is possessive in the surface but read as a plain plural
definitions.meaning: second meaning: flat discs with a hole, used under nuts and bolts

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe makes it look as if the rings belong to the scrubbers; it is just two meanings side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone who cleans is a washer, and the small flat metal or rubber discs that seal joints are also called washers.

clue.text: Isn't about English, of course

parts.note: ain't is the informal form of isn't
re means about, concerning
standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone insists that, naturally, something has nothing to do with English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like a throwaway 'naturally', but course is the definition: Aintree is the Liverpool racecourse that hosts the Grand National.
explanation.definitionFit: Aintree is a famous horse-racing course near Liverpool, so it is an example of a racecourse.

clue.text: Rogues' gallery, content to contribute

parts.note: an imp is a little rogue or rascal
art is what fills a gallery

explanation.surface: A rogues' gallery of police mugshots is happy to be put to use.
explanation.walkthrough: A rogues' gallery is a police collection of photos of known criminals; here the phrase is split into a rogue and what a gallery holds.
explanation.definitionFit: To impart is to give or pass on, such as knowledge or a quality, which is what contributing something does.

clue.text: Authors plot roles to be developed

indicators.note: something still to be developed is unfinished and will be reshaped, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Novelists sketch out a storyline with characters still to be fleshed out.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Trollope and his mother Frances were both Victorian novelists, so the plural surname covers a family of authors.
explanation.definitionFit: The Trollopes, Anthony and Frances, were mother and son who each wrote many popular nineteenth-century novels.

clue.text: Artist and composer cutting a green

indicators.note: cutting something out removes it, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: Edward Elgar, the English composer
taken as written; this is the letter removed
eco- means environmentally friendly, or green

explanation.surface: A painter and a composer are out mowing a patch of lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artist and composer' looks like two people, but the artist is the definition and the composer loses his A before the green is added.
explanation.definitionFit: El Greco was the Cretan-born painter who worked in Spain, famous for elongated, dramatic religious figures.

clue.text: Police omitted alteration, a waste of space!

indicators.note: an alteration is a change, so the letters are changed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone fumes that the police skipped a change and calls the result useless.
explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is printed with a comma (8,5), but the answer is the phrase 'complete idiot'.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a waste of space is a scornful insult meaning they are useless, the same put-down as utter fool.

clue.text: Found in caddy or kitchen bowl

indicators.note: something found in a place is sitting inside it, so the letters lie within the words that follow

parts.note: spans the end of the first word, the middle word and the start of the last

explanation.surface: Something turns up in the tea caddy or a mixing bowl in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kitchen bowl' looks like a mixing bowl; bowl is a cricket verb. A yorker is a ball pitched at the batter's feet, and to york someone is to bowl them out with one. York also has a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket, to york a batsman is to dismiss them with a yorker, a delivery aimed right at the feet.

clue.text: Show up long moving vehicle

indicators.note: things that are moving change position, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A lengthy truck in motion makes an appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long moving vehicle' looks like one phrase for a lorry, but long belongs to the letters and moving is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A snowplough is a truck or machine fitted with a blade for clearing snow from roads, so it is a kind of vehicle.

clue.text: Web reveals tense affair

parts.note: standard grammatical abbreviation for tense
an issue is a matter or affair

explanation.surface: The internet exposes a strained romance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Web' and 'affair' suggest online scandal; web means an interwoven fabric, and 'tense' is just the grammatical letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tissue is a fine woven fabric or an interlinked mass, as in a tissue of lies, which is what a web is.

clue.text: Similar cultured pearl everyone collected

indicators.note: to collect something is to gather it in, so one piece is held inside another
something cultured has been worked on and refined, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
all means everyone

explanation.surface: Everyone gathered up matching cultured pearls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cultured pearl' is a real jewellery term, which hides that cultured is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Parallel can describe things that correspond or run alongside each other closely, so it means alike or comparable.

clue.text: Decoration 28 lost — hard cheese!

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers

indicators.note: what is lost is no longer there, so a letter goes missing

parts.note: the answer to 28 across
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard; this letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone lost a medal and is told 'hard cheese', British slang for tough luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard cheese!' reads as a stock phrase of mock sympathy, but hard is the letter dropped from CHESTER. Red Leicester is a firm English cheese, and Leicester also has a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Leicester, usually Red Leicester, is a firm orange English cow's-milk cheese named after its home county.

clue.text: Fine, but lacking a server?

parts.note: the cloud is the internet's network of remote servers
the suffix -less means without

explanation.surface: A restaurant is fine except that nobody is waiting at table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Server' points to a waiter; here it is computing storage. Fine is weather, not quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine weather is bright and dry, and a sky with no clouds at all is the clearest example of that.

clue.text: Salts — keep some supplies

indicators.note: to supply is to provide what is held in store, so the letters come from inside the words given

parts.note: runs from inside the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A note to keep a stock of salts in reserve.
explanation.walkthrough: Salts is not the definition of a chemical; Epsom salts are the bath crystals, and Epsom Downs is the Surrey racecourse of the Derby.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom salts are magnesium sulphate crystals, named after the Surrey town where the mineral spring was found, so Epsom completes the phrase.

clue.text: An English neighbour's tie

parts.note: the indefinite article
Scotland borders England

explanation.surface: An Englishman's next-door neighbour wears a necktie.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks possessive but stands for 'is'. Ascot is also the Berkshire racecourse of Royal Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: An ascot is a broad formal cravat worn at the neck, named after the racecourse where it was fashionable.

clue.text: Put up with dashing moustache, but not posh face of emperor

indicators.note: dashing about means rushing in all directions, so the letters are scattered
'but not' means excluding, so letters are taken away

parts.note: taken as written
U means upper-class, as in U and non-U

indicators.note: the face is the front, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Someone tolerates a dashing moustache, though not a posh one on an emperor's face.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove U and E from MOUSTACHE, then rearrange the remaining seven letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To stomach something is to tolerate or endure it, the idiom being that one can digest it.

clue.text: City team huddle together around first toilet

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: to nestle is to snuggle close together
WC is water closet
A is first, as in A1 or grade A

explanation.surface: A football squad gathers in a huddle round the main toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: Newcastle is a city in north-east England and also its football club; it also has a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Newcastle is both a northern English city and the shorthand name of its football club, Newcastle United.

clue.text: Laugh, eating end of ginger snap

indicators.note: what is eaten goes inside the eater, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: to cackle is to laugh shrilly

indicators.note: the end is the final part, so only the last letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of this word

explanation.surface: Someone laughs while munching a ginger snap biscuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ginger snap' looks like the biscuit, but snap is the definition and ginger only gives its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A crackle is a sharp crisp popping sound, the same noise as a snap made by twigs or a fire.

clue.text: A gun destroyed by soldiers after conclusive metal fatigue

indicators.note: conclusive refers to the conclusion, so the final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of this word

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken apart, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
OR is Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A gun is wrecked by troops after it is proved the metal has weakened.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Metal fatigue' is a real engineering term that hides the definition at the end; 'after' puts the soldiers last.
explanation.definitionFit: Languor is a pleasant or heavy weariness and lack of energy, which is what fatigue means.

clue.text: Spooner's refusal of engagement present

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words

parts.note: a refusal is a no; it takes the D sound from the next word
an engagement is a date; it takes the N sound from the word before

explanation.surface: Spooner turns down an invitation and offers a gift instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of NO DATE. 'Present' looks like a noun (a gift) but must be read as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To present something is to hand it over formally as a gift, which is what donating means.

clue.text: Speedy festival, gash maybe

parts.note: surface reading: a gash is a deep cut
setter's reading: G is short for good, and ASH is an example of a wood, so the answer's two halves shrink to these letters

explanation.surface: A cut picked up at a fast-paced festival.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: abbreviate the answer's halves and you get G plus ASH. The Goodwood Festival of Speed is a motoring event in Sussex, and Goodwood also has a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Goodwood in West Sussex hosts the annual Festival of Speed, a celebration of fast cars and motor racing.

clue.text: A race with one French condition

parts.note: taken as written
the TT is the Isle of Man Tourist Trophy motorcycle race
une is French for one (feminine)

explanation.surface: A race run with a French entrant in a certain state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Condition' looks like a noun but is the verb: to accustom or adjust.
explanation.definitionFit: To attune someone is to accustom or adjust them to something, which is what conditioning them does.

clue.text: Pulse in borscht served up, self-catering failed

indicators.note: in a down clue, served up means turned upwards, so the letters run bottom to top
something that has failed is no longer present, so those letters drop out

parts.note: taken as written
SC is the holiday-listing abbreviation for self-catering

explanation.surface: Pulses in a beetroot soup are dished out after a do-it-yourself cooking attempt went wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' looks like lentils in the soup; it is a heartbeat. Borscht is a beetroot soup from eastern Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: A throb is a strong regular beat, like the pulse of the heart felt in the wrist or temples.

clue.text: Picture technique of former PM not dealing with American Jobs

indicators.note: 'not' excludes something, so those letters are left out

parts.note: David Cameron, UK Prime Minister 2010 to 2016
on means about, concerning; these letters are removed
standard abbreviation for American
jobs collectively are work

explanation.surface: A former prime minister's approach to photography, avoiding American job questions.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital on 'Jobs' suggests Steve Jobs of Apple; it is just plain work.
explanation.definitionFit: Camerawork is the way a film or photograph is shot, the craft of handling the camera.

clue.text: Fish, once head is removed, is best

indicators.note: removing the head takes off the front, so the opening letter goes

parts.note: a trout is a freshwater fish

explanation.surface: Fish taste best once beheaded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like an adjective about taste; it is the verb meaning to defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: To rout an opponent is to defeat them heavily, and to best someone means to beat or outdo them.

clue.text: Former president shows way to shout about

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: to cheer is to shout encouragement
St is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: An ex-president demonstrates how to yell about something.
explanation.walkthrough: Chester A Arthur was the 21st US president, known by his first name here. Chester also has England's oldest racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Chester Arthur served as US president in the 1880s, so his first name stands for a former president.

clue.text: This makes Ruby appear in market town

parts.note: surface reading: something that brings a woman called Ruby out into town
setter's reading: a market town's name, rearranged, spells the woman's name, and 'new' is the rearrangement signal that does it

explanation.surface: Something persuades a woman named Ruby to show up in a market town.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as an instruction, NEW (rearrange) the letters of BURY, a Lancashire town, and RUBY appears. Newbury in Berkshire is itself a market town with a racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Newbury is a Berkshire town that grew up around its market and is famous for its racecourse.
